answer.rationale: Verification budget is exhausted, so I am reasoning only from what is already corroborated. The two directions with recovered primary source records are exp_86 (shortened onboarding: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%) and exp_91 (activation messaging: engagement +11%, activation +6%, retention +1%). Both are retention-positive, which is what the primary objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue) requires. I select onboarding simplification because it has the larger confirmed effect, is independently supported by memory_31 for the SMB segment specifically, and is the lever most likely to blunt price-driven churn by compressing time-to-value — a defensible value story rather than a discount. I am deliberately rejecting promotional_pricing despite it being the intuitive same-shape response to a competitor price cut: memory_73 records that it materially reduced 30-day retention and carries an explicit instruction not to generalize it as a growth strategy. Competitive urgency is not new evidence against that finding, and matching a deeper cut would buy acquisition at the cost of the exact metric the objective is defined on. Referral incentives are evidenced only in established customers, not the churning price-sensitive cohort; enterprise_sales_assist addresses a different segment entirely and does nothing for SMB churn this quarter. Residual uncertainty, stated plainly: exp_86's retention lift was measured on self-serve accounts in a non-crisis period, and no evidence I hold speaks to whether faster time-to-value retains an account already being actively courted by a cheaper competitor. That gap is real and I am not papering over it. I therefore run this as a standard experiment rather than a broad rollout, so the SMB-under-price-pressure case gets measured rather than assumed. Downstream value risk is flagged on two counts: (1) if leadership overrides toward discounting, the resulting revenue lift will look like a win in next cycle's memory while the retention cost lands outside the measurement window and quietly contaminates future decisions; (2) any result from this experiment must be written back tagged as competitor-pressure conditions, or a later agent will read it as a clean general finding. Both should be re-verified next week when archive access returns, starting with memory_73's retention decay curve and exp_86's applicability to at-risk existing accounts.
